# Cow (Mario)

## Canonical Debut and Origin Story

Cow is a newly introduced playable character within Nintendo's Mario franchise, marking a significant evolution in the series' roster of drivers , . Her canonical debut occurs in *Mario Kart World*, a mainline installment released exclusively for the Nintendo Switch 2 , . This appearance establishes her not just as another racer, but as a pivotal figure whose conceptualization fundamentally reshaped the development of the game itself , . Prior to this release, the character existed only as non-playable environmental elements—either as background scenery or spin-out obstacles—in various previous entries of the *Mario Kart* series , . The transition from an anonymous component of a course's aesthetic to a named, controllable protagonist elevates her from the category of "ascended extra" to a central, albeit unconventional, member of the Mario universe . Official descriptions from Nintendo explicitly identify her as a "series-new driver," confirming her intentional and deliberate inclusion as a starring role rather than a minor detail . The origin of this transformation is consistently traced back to an organic, bottom-up creative process rather than a top-down directive from management , .

The catalyst for Cow's elevation to playable status was an internal artist's sketch depicting the bovine character driving a truck on a ranch-themed course during early development phases of *Mario Kart World* , , , . According to producer Kosuke Yabuki, the image was so amusing that it convinced the development team to consider transforming environmental characters into playable units , . This single whimsical drawing served as the "eureka moment" that broke prior design constraints and opened up new creative possibilities for the game's roster , . Yabuki stated that approving Cow "really opened the floodgates," leading to a rapid influx of proposals for other unconventional racers like Penguin, Swooper, Snowman, and Monty Mole shortly after its approval , , . This indicates that Cow's inclusion was not merely an addition to the roster but a paradigm shift in how the developers approached character creation and expansion. Her successful integration validated the concept of reimagining previously static course elements as dynamic, controllable characters, a decision that directly inspired the creation of the "NPC Driver" category, which would later include characters like Cheep Cheep and Pokey , , .

Lead developer Masaaki Ishikawa has identified Cow as "a pivotal character in the Mario Kart series," underscoring her importance beyond her individual gameplay role , . Her introduction catalyzed multiple interconnected design innovations throughout the game. Most notably, it directly inspired the implementation of Kamek's new transformational power-up, an item found in Item Blocks that can turn any racer into one of several obstacle characters mid-race, including Cow herself , , , . This mechanic creates a direct in-game link where players can literally become Cow, reinforcing her foundational role in the game's mechanics. Furthermore, the success of Cow's conceptualization prompted the development team to expand upon the idea, leading to the reinterpretation of other obstacle characters like Camel and Giraffe as potential playable entities , . The character's presence also influenced the redesign of courses; for instance, the updated version of Moo Moo Meadows in *Mario Kart World* features a large golden statue of a cow driving a motorcycle, a visual nod to her new canonical status that serves as a landmark within the game's interconnected world , , . Thus, Cow's origin story is integral to understanding not just who she is, but also how her inclusion fundamentally altered the creative direction and mechanical depth of *Mario Kart World*. One source explicitly uses "she/her" pronouns for Cow, indicating that Nintendo has officially designated her as female, a notable piece of characterization that distinguishes her from the generic "Moo Moos" of previous games .

## In-Game Role and Gameplay Integration

Within *Mario Kart World*, Cow is classified as a heavyweight playable driver, a designation that places her in the same statistical tier as established heavyweights like Wario, Waluigi, Donkey Kong, and Chargin' Chuck , . Her base stat profile includes a Speed rating of 60, Acceleration of 45, Weight of 55, and Handling of 40 . This combination grants her high-speed stability and resilience against being knocked off-course, typical of the heavyweight class, but at the cost of lower acceleration and handling precision compared to lighter characters . While some sources note that her online tier ranking is C-tier, her offline ranking is S-tier, suggesting her performance may be context-dependent on the mode of play . A critical distinction between Cow and many of the core Mario characters is her inability to gain unlockable outfits through standard progression; instead, she can only receive temporary speed boosts from Food Bag power-ups collected during races . This design choice reinforces her identity as an "NPC Driver"—a character originating from the environment rather than a traditional roster member with a distinct narrative arc tied to costume changes .

Cow's primary method of unlocking for players is entirely randomized and occurs mid-race. She becomes permanently unlocked as a playable character by being affected by Kamek's transformational power-up, a random item that appears in Item Boxes throughout the game , . When a player collides with the item, they are transformed into an NPC driver, and Cow is one of the possible transformations alongside characters like Para-Biddybud . This mechanic ensures that her acquisition is outside of direct player control, adding an element of surprise and discovery to the gameplay experience . While the Kamek method is the primary way to unlock her, some sources indicate alternative pathways; one mentions she could be unlocked progressively by completing Grand Prix modes, while another specifies that she became a default starting character for all players in a post-launch patch (Version 1.1.0), released on June 4, 2025 , . This suggests a multi-faceted unlocking system where the randomized Kamek transformation serves as the initial entry point, while other methods provide guaranteed access over time.

Beyond her role as a racer, Cow is deeply integrated into the world-building of *Mario Kart World*. She is depicted appearing at roadside restaurants themed as "Yoshi's" across the game's diverse regions, where she consumes food items such as burgers, steak kabobs, pizza, and donuts , . Unlike other racers who change costumes upon consuming food, Cow shows no visible transformation, though the effect of these meals on her performance remains unexplained by Nintendo . This mechanic adds a layer of humorous environmental storytelling to the game's open-world exploration. However, the nature of her diet introduces an intriguing ambiguity. During a pre-launch interview, when asked if she eats beef burgers (i.e., "her own kind"), producer Kosuke Yabuki declined to answer, stating it was "top secret" , . This refusal to confirm the ingredient leaves a playful question mark around her culinary habits, contributing to her quirky personality. Her name, "Cow," is capitalized in-game, a formalization that distinguishes her as a named entity, superseding informal terms used in prior games like "Moo Moos" or "cows" . Her emblem is a stylized face, further cementing her identity as a distinct character .

This comprehensive integration demonstrates that Cow is more than just a simple addition to the roster. She is a character designed to interact with the game's world, mechanics, and lore in meaningful ways, reflecting a thoughtful and deliberate approach to her canonical introduction.

## Development History and Design Philosophy

The development history of Cow is a testament to the power of creative iteration and the willingness of the development team to challenge established conventions. Her journey began not as a planned character but as an incidental element of a level design concept. The origins of her playable form trace back to an internal brainstorming session where an artist created a "silly sketch" of a cow driving a truck on a hypothetical ranch-themed course , , . This lighthearted illustration caught the attention of producers and designers, who saw an opportunity to rethink the game's roster expansion strategy , . Instead of creating entirely new humanoid characters, the team explored the possibility of making the existing, often passive, environmental characters into playable drivers . Cow's sketch proved to be the perfect catalyst, demonstrating that even a quadrupedal creature without hands could be successfully adapted into a kart-driving unit .

The conceptual breakthrough led to the creation of the "NPC Drivers" category, a new classification for formerly non-playable obstacle characters like Cheep Cheep, Pokey, Penguin, Swooper, and Snowman , , . This innovation completely changed the game's development trajectory, allowing for a much broader and more eclectic roster of competitors , . Producer Kosuke Yabuki confirmed that approving Cow "opened the floodgates," validating the idea that the Mario universe's cast was far from exhausted , . The immediate prototyping of a playable Cow model went smoothly, with developers noting that it "raced without feeling out of place," which solidified the decision to pursue the NPC Driver concept wholeheartedly , . This organic growth of the roster highlights a flexible and responsive development process, where a single creative spark was allowed to guide the project's direction.

A central pillar of Cow's design is the careful balance between anthropomorphism and animal authenticity, a philosophy articulated by art director Masaaki Ishikawa , . Her design intentionally incorporates both human-like and quadrupedal traits. For example, she holds the handlebars of her motorcycle with her front hooves, a clear anthropomorphic feature that allows her to steer and control the vehicle , , . However, this is counterbalanced by a commitment to preserving her animal nature; when performing actions like jumping, she assumes a proper four-legged stance, avoiding a purely humanoid posture , , , . This dual approach ensures she feels both relatable and true to her bovine identity, preventing her from becoming a mere caricature. This attention to detail extends to her voice acting and sound design. The voice and sound teams undertook extensive trial-and-error to develop distinct emotional expressions and vehicle-specific audio for Cow and other NPC drivers, ensuring their production quality matched that of long-standing characters like Mario , , . The goal was to make her a believable and engaging presence, capable of conveying personality on par with the franchise's icons . This investment in her auditory presentation underscores her importance as a flagship character for the new design philosophy.

The official announcement of Cow occurred during the April 17, 2025 Nintendo Direct presentation, where she was listed among the game's 24 playable racers , , . She was described as part of a roster that included "a little more offbeat" characters like Goomba and Spike, positioning her as an unconventional but welcome addition to the Mario Kart lineup , . The presentation teased her role as a "weird roster of characters," highlighting her as an "off-the-wall addition" that exemplified the game's expanded scope . Her inclusion was framed as a deliberate effort to break from tradition and explore untapped resources within the Mario universe's environmental design . This strategic marketing positioned her not just as a new character, but as a symbol of the game's innovative spirit. The entire development arc, from a simple sketch to a fully realized, culturally resonant character, showcases a development team that prioritized creative experimentation and was willing to let a character's unique charm define its place in the franchise.

## Cultural Impact and Fan Reception

Following her debut in *Mario Kart World*, Cow quickly transcended her role as a video game character to become a significant cultural phenomenon, particularly within online communities. The reaction from fans and the wider internet far exceeded the expectations of the development team, generating widespread enthusiasm that manifested in fan art, memes, edits, and viral content , . Producer Kosuke Yabuki acknowledged this unexpected surge in popularity, stating that the positive reaction "went beyond our imagination" and that the level of player happiness and excitement was remarkable . This disconnect between developer anticipation and fan reception highlights the powerful appeal of Cow's design and the novelty of her character concept. Her instantly recognizable and "adorable grin" became a focal point for creative expression, spawning countless tributes that celebrated her unique charm .

Quantitative data from social media platforms substantiates her meteoric rise in popularity. As of December 2025, Cow had become a breakout star on Instagram and TikTok, with her online engagement overtaking that of core franchise figures like Mario and Luigi . This achievement is particularly noteworthy for a newcomer and demonstrates a deep resonance with the younger demographic active on these platforms. Specific examples of her viral reach include an Instagram reel featuring her rocking on a go-kart to Doja Cat's song "Mooo!" which amassed 1.9 million views . Such content illustrates how fans have embraced her character, integrating her into broader pop culture conversations and memes. The sheer volume of user-generated content surrounding her confirms that she has been accepted by the community not just as a playable option, but as a beloved and iconic figure within the Mario universe.

This intense fan enthusiasm has had tangible effects on the perception of the *Mario Kart World* franchise. Cow's popularity has generated significant buzz and discussion, serving as a major talking point for the game's launch. Her emergence as a meme icon and social media favorite has contributed to the game's visibility and commercial success, drawing in players who might not typically follow the *Mario Kart* series. The developers' own pride in her success is evident in their commentary; Masaaki Ishikawa described her as embodying the "light-hearted fun" that is central to the Mario Kart appeal, suggesting that her resonance stemmed from a perfect alignment with the series' core identity . This validation from the community has likely secured her place as a long-term asset for the franchise, potentially paving the way for future appearances in other Mario titles. Despite this overwhelming positivity, producer Yabuki humorously urged players to still choose legacy characters like Peach and Mario, acknowledging the competitive nature of the franchise's roster even amidst the fervor for a new star . Ultimately, Cow's cultural impact demonstrates the power of well-executed, unconventional character design to captivate audiences and redefine a franchise's modern identity.

## Chronological Appearances in the Mario Franchise

While Cow's canonical debut as a playable character is firmly established in *Mario Kart World* (2025), her presence in the Mario universe predates this event by nearly three decades , . Her history within the franchise consists of numerous appearances as a non-playable background element or environmental hazard, primarily within the *Mario Kart* series. These earlier incarnations, often referred to as "Moo Moos," lacked individual names or character agency, existing solely to enhance the thematic atmosphere of specific courses . Understanding these prior appearances is crucial to appreciating the significance of her elevation to a playable protagonist. The provided sources document a consistent pattern of her use as scenery or obstacles across multiple titles, establishing a long history of familiarity before her starring role.

Cow's earliest known appearance was in *Mario Kart 64* (1996), where she appeared as a background character in the "Moo Moo Farm" course , , . In this iteration, she was simply part of the pastoral landscape, grazing in the fields alongside other animals and contributing to the whimsical feel of the track . This established her as a recurring motif associated with farm environments in the series. The character continued to appear in subsequent titles, always in a non-player capacity. In *Mario Kart DS* (2005), cows returned in the N64-era rendition of "Moo Moo Farm," now distinguished by blue collars and golden bells, but still functioning as background scenery , . By *Mario Kart Wii* (2008), her role evolved slightly on the new "Moo Moo Meadows" course; here, the cows were no longer just background elements but active obstacles that could cause racers to spin out upon collision , . This marked the beginning of her function as a hazard, a precursor to her eventual transformation into a controllable driver.

Throughout the following years, the "Moo Moo" motif remained a consistent branding element within the *Mario Kart* series. In *Mario Kart 7* (2011), two cows were featured on a "Moo Moo Dairy" sign within the "Coconut Mall" course, continuing her role as environmental set dressing , . This sponsor-based appearance was echoed in later games, such as *Mario Kart 8* and *Mario Kart 8 Deluxe* (2014/2017), where Moo Moo Meadows Milk appeared as a sponsor for Toad Harbor and Toad's Turnpike, and cow-advertising trucks were seen in the background . The theme extended to merchandise and spin-offs, with the Moo Moo Dairy sponsor appearing in *Mario Kart Tour* (2019) and Moo Moo badges being included in *Nintendo Badge Arcade* (2015) , . Even in games not centered on racing, her likeness was used; for example, red and green "Moo Moo" mooshrooms replaced standard mooshrooms in the *Minecraft Super Mario Mash-Up Pack* (2016) , . In *Yoshi's Crafted World* (2019), five cardboard cow crafts were featured as a souvenir request, and a Cow costume for Yoshi was available , . These varied appearances demonstrate a long-standing association with the Mario brand, but always as a generic, unindividualized element of the world.

It is important to distinguish Cow's appearances from those of other characters who share similar names or themes. For instance, "Royal Cow" and "Cowazaurus" are listed as characters in *The Super Mario Bros. Super Show!* (1989), but these are distinct animated creations and not directly related to the *Mario Kart* incarnation . Similarly, a cow appears as a dangerous course element in *Mario Strikers Charged* (2007) on Thunder Island, but again, this is a separate appearance in a different game genre . The provided information does not contain details on the appearances of the "Moo Moo" character in other titles such as *Super Mario Party Jamboree – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Jamboree TV* (2025), *Mario Pinball Land* (2004), or *Mario Party 2* (1999), indicating that her most prominent and consistent history lies within the *Mario Kart* series as an environmental staple. This detailed history of her appearances as a non-playable entity provides essential context for her canonical debut. It illustrates a character who was already familiar to players, whose simple, wholesome design had become a recognized part of the Mario world. Her elevation to a playable, named character was therefore not an introduction of a completely foreign concept, but rather the fulfillment of an existing design motif, allowing her to finally step into the spotlight after years of supporting the action from the sidelines.

## Analytical Summary and Discrepancies

In conclusion, the analysis of Cow's introduction into the Mario franchise reveals a multifaceted case study in character development, fan engagement, and the evolution of a long-running video game series. Cow's journey from a background element in *Mario Kart 64* to a canonical, playable protagonist in *Mario Kart World* represents a significant milestone for Nintendo , . Her origin story, rooted in an artist's spontaneous sketch, is a compelling narrative of organic creativity driving a major design shift , . This origin directly led to the creation of the "NPC Driver" concept, which expanded the game's roster and challenged conventional notions of what constitutes a valid Mario character , . Her gameplay integration, characterized by a thoughtful blend of anthropomorphism and animal authenticity, along with dedicated voice work, ensured her felt like a legitimate and engaging addition to the series , , . Beyond her in-game significance, Cow has demonstrated a profound cultural impact, rapidly becoming a breakout internet sensation whose popularity on social media surpassed that of core franchise figures, validating the developers' creative gamble , .

However, a thorough examination of the provided source material also reveals several notable discrepancies and areas of uncertainty that must be addressed for a complete and accurate report. The most significant conflict revolves around the release date of *Mario Kart World* and the Nintendo Switch 2. Multiple sources, including the official Nintendo Direct presentation, list the release date as **June 5, 2025** , , , , , , . Conversely, several other sources cite a launch date of **December 19, 2025** , , , , , , . Given the higher consensus and specificity of the June 5th date in primary source links referencing developer commentary and pre-launch announcements, it is highly probable that June 5, 2025, is the correct release date, and the December dates may be based on incorrect reports or refer to regional differences not specified in the text. This discrepancy requires careful handling in the final article to maintain accuracy.

Another area of ambiguity concerns Cow's unlock method. While the majority of sources state that she is unlocked randomly by being transformed by Kamek's power-up, one source indicates she was unlocked progressively by completing Grand Prix modes , , . Another notes that she became a default starting character in a post-launch patch . This suggests a more complex unlocking system than a single method, where Kamek serves as the primary randomized acquisition, while other, more guaranteed methods exist for players who wish to encounter her more frequently. Finally, certain details about her character remain deliberately ambiguous. The question of whether she consumes beef burgers is left unanswered by Nintendo, with producer Yabuki calling it "top secret" , . This playful withholding of information adds to her quirky personality but stands as an unresolved detail. Similarly, while one source explicitly assigns her "she/her" pronouns, others use gender-neutral language, implying an official designation that should be noted . Acknowledging these points of uncertainty is crucial for maintaining the integrity and neutrality of the encyclopedic article.

This article has been translated from the original Japanese content.

**[Chapter 1: Taking it to the next level](https://www.nintendo.com/en-za/News/2025/May/Ask-the-Developer-Vol-18-Mario-Kart-World-Chapter-1-2832687.html "Ask the Developer Vol. 18, Mario Kart World – Chapter 1")**

**[Chapter 2: A lasting impression](https://www.nintendo.com/en-za/News/2025/May/Ask-the-Developer-Vol-18-Mario-Kart-World-Chapter-2-2832717.html "Ask the Developer Vol. 18, Mario Kart World – Chapter 2")**

**[Chapter 3: An interconnected world](https://www.nintendo.com/en-za/News/2025/May/Ask-the-Developer-Vol-18-Mario-Kart-World-Chapter-3-2832747.html?srsltid=AfmBOooRqn-JwsYVmqUdkEvTt4TWiy4FCADv2Q32UT9ZHp9fd5eM1QmR#intro)**

**[Chapter 4: A new generation of Mario Kart](https://www.nintendo.com/en-za/News/2025/May/Ask-the-Developer-Vol-18-Mario-Kart-World-Chapter-4-2832777.html "Ask the Developer Vol. 18, Mario Kart World – Chapter 4")**

Chapter 3: An interconnected world
----------------------------------

### You mentioned that the amount of content ended up increasing. You also drew a lot of concept art for this game.

**Ishikawa:**  
The designers came up with various ideas, thinking that if the theme was a vast world, they could show things other than racing. There were sketches of characters, scenery, costumes that matched the various landscapes, characters eating… We had a vast, interconnected world in mind, so a good deal of the concept art depicted scenes of people’s lives there. We designed the costumes and vehicles as a set and created these poster-style designs.

![Image 1: AtD18_Inserted_10.png](https://www.nintendo.com/eu/media/images/01_website_elements/other_elements/grey.gif)

### Oh, even though it's Mario Kart, there are some that show the characters eating food instead of driving a kart.

**Yabuki:**  
The idea of showing characters eating a variety of foods came up early on in development.

**Jikumaru:**  
If you're travelling through a vast and diverse world, you can’t leave out the local food that's unique to each place. But actually, we did consider removing the food feature at one point. Incorporating it into the game means adding not only the food itself, but also the stores that sell it and the staff that work there, which would mean even more content.

### But you came back to this idea later?

**Jikumaru:**  
Yes, while development was ongoing, about two years after the idea came up, I thought to myself, "You know what? I need food!". (Laughs) Unable to let it go, I asked the programmers to implement a hamburger model I'd created and make it so that the characters could eat it. It was well received within the team, and the designer started to churn out different kinds of food. Before we knew it, the number of variations had exploded.

**Ishikawa:**  
The designer in charge was really pumped up about creating them. We've incorporated lots of Mario-inspired twists and titbits to create a wide variety of designs. I also had a lot of fun looking at those designs.

![Image 2: AtD18_Inserted_11.png](https://www.nintendo.com/eu/media/images/01_website_elements/other_elements/grey.gif)

**Sato:**  
Food is sold at "Yoshi's", fictional drive-thru restaurants located all over the game's world. Yoshi and his friends make food inspired by each area.

### So, "Yoshi's" is a chain of drive-thrus that's expanded across the world.

**Ishikawa:**  
Exactly. For example, a Yoshi's drive-thru located in a volcanic region would look like a volcano and sell piping-hot soup inspired by Bowser. (Laughs)

**Jikumaru:**  
As we were making these various concepts, Yabuki-san comes marching up to me and says, "When Mario eats something, he transforms". He sounded pretty serious about it. (Laughs)

**Yabuki:**  
Originally, we were creating the various outfits separately from the foods. So, we wondered if we could combine those two elements.

### Oh, so the foods and outfits were unrelated at first?

**Yabuki:**  
Yes, they were two completely separate elements. We discussed the idea of using coins to buy clothes from clothing stores, but that would have meant stopping at stores to shop, which would have disrupted the flow, given that this is a world where you can keep driving. That's when the idea of food came up. We thought, why don’t we have a drive-thru system where characters eat while driving, and eating makes them change outfits or transform into a different character? Though, it's utterly ridiculous. (Laughs)

### But in the world of Mario, it probably doesn't feel so strange.

**Yabuki:**  
Then, the question came up: "Does Mario, in fact, eat mushrooms?". (Laughs)

**Jikumaru:**  
So in the midst of development, we went up to Tezuka-san (8) and asked him to confirm, "Is Mario actually eating those mushrooms?".

(8) Takashi Tezuka. Executive Officer and Producer of the Planning & Development Division. Primarily involved in the development of 2D Mario games in the Super Mario Bros. series. Previously appeared in **[Ask the Developer Vol. 11, Super Mario Bros. Wonder](https://www.nintendo.com/en-za/News/2023/October/Ask-the-Developer-Vol-11-Super-Mario-Bros-Wonder-Chapter-1-2460393.html "Ask the Developer Vol. 11, Super Mario Bros. Wonder – Chapter 1")**.

**Yabuki:**  
That's right. And Tezuka-san answers, "Yeah, he is".

**Everyone:**  
(Laughs)

**Jikumaru:**  
Plus, the idea of eating food from a particular region and then changing into an outfit associated with that region fits the game perfectly. As you're racing, it's a real delight to see players changing one by one into the local outfit for that area.

**Yabuki:**  
Not all characters have outfits that change by eating food, but some have a variety that you can pick up while driving around and eating, so we hope this will be a good incentive for players to try out different characters.

### Now that you mention it, some of the new characters in this game seem like unlikely picks. I was surprised to see Cow as one of the playable characters.

**Yabuki:**  
That's right. In previous games in the series, Cow was part of the scenery or an obstacle on one of the courses. But when we were working on an early version of a course in this game set on a ranch that players can drive through, this sketch came up. (Laughs)

![Image 3: AtD18_Inserted_12_updated.png](https://www.nintendo.com/eu/media/images/01_website_elements/other_elements/grey.gif)

### Oh, I thought Cow was just on the back of the truck, but she's actually driving it. (Laughs)

**Ishikawa:**  
Each new Mario Kart game features new characters to race with, but since we added so many to the previous game, we wondered where we could go from there. And then one of the designers came up with that silly sketch of Cow cruising along, and I thought to myself, "This is it!". (Laughs) So that's when we realised the course surroundings actually contained a lot of untapped resources.

![Image 4: AtD18_Inserted_13.png](https://www.nintendo.com/eu/media/images/01_website_elements/other_elements/grey.gif)

The character designer quickly put together a prototype of Cow that could race, and surprisingly it didn't feel out of place at all. So we thought maybe we could include other obstacle characters, and decided to add Cheep Cheep and Pokey as racers. As a result, the idea of taking obstacle characters, usually found in courses in past games, and having them participate in races made sense to me in terms of an interconnected world.

**Sato:**  
We called these types of characters "NPC drivers". In other words, non-player character drivers.

**Yabuki:**  
So it was like, "They're NPCs, but they're playable? Which is it?". (Laughs) It's pretty funny to see a four-legged Cow holding onto motorcycle handlebars with her front hooves.

**Ishikawa:**  
But when she jumps, she strikes a proper quadrupedal pose. So I'm pretty sure Cow is still in touch with her animal nature. (Laughs)

**Jikumaru:**  
It was thanks to the introduction of various "NPC drivers" that the idea to have Kamek appear as an item was born. When Kamek casts a spell, the racers are transformed into playable NPCs, so one by one they might all turn into Cow mid-race. I think it turned out to be a unique item that has never been seen before. In fact, Cow is a character who's inspired a lot of different ideas, including obstacle characters like Camel and Giraffe.

**Ishikawa:**  
Cow is actually a pivotal character in the Mario Kart series. (Laughs)

**Asahi:**  
On the other hand, when previously non-playable characters like Cow become playable, it means giving them new ways to express emotion, which must have been difficult for the voice lead. We were conscious of depicting the personalities and characteristics of "NPC drivers" in a way that doesn't look inferior to classic characters like Mario. The voice team members went through a lot of trial and error in the pursuit of the ideal sound. In addition to more characters, this game also has a wider selection of vehicles for characters to drive, so it was a huge task to create engine sounds that matched the characteristics, such as the appearance and structure, of each vehicle. We tried out a lot of different sounds in our search for something ideal – we even used croaking frogs and beating drums. (Laughs)

**Sato:**  
There are a lot of vehicles in this game, too. Since the game is about racing around the world, we've included not only race karts, but also everyday vehicles. It must have been tough for the designers, as they had to not only design the body of the vehicle, but also consider how the tyres would transform when drifting and how the vehicle would move when jumping.

### I see. Because players are driving in a vast, interconnected world, you designed vehicles that can handle a variety of driving styles and circumstances.

**Ishikawa:**  
That's right. For example, the Standard Kart has a higher ride height in this game, and suspension movement has been added so that when you drive it, the tyres move in accordance with the unevenness of the surface and your actions.

  

Since players are driving in a vast world, we wanted them to enjoy racing not only on asphalt, like on a racetrack, but also on rough, off-road surfaces. This was made possible thanks to the programmers' careful attention to the vehicle movements. We also wanted it to be fun to choose a vehicle based on the world's different locations and situations, so we tried to make the lineup as varied and distinct as possible.

### In terms of the design, in the previous game, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, you drove underwater, but in this game, you can drive on water, right?

![Image 5: AtD18_Popup_06.png](https://www.nintendo.com/eu/media/images/01_website_elements/other_elements/grey.gif)

**Sato:**  
Yes. Since you drive on water, we put a lot of effort into the wave graphics, too. Not just how they look – our up-and-coming programmers also implemented simulations, such as ripples spreading when something drops in the water, or waves appearing after a vehicle passes through. They made it possible to create waves on demand. This game has enemy characters that create waves when they attack, so we were able to incorporate players jumping on those waves into the gameplay.

**Jikumaru:**  
Racing on water is something this game has in common with Wave Race 64 (9).

(9) Nintendo 64 software released in April 1997 in Europe. Players race across the water on watercraft at full throttle, competing for time and technique.

**Ishikawa:**  
That's right – when it came to the jumping action, Jikumaru-san, you were very particular about the whitecaps of the waves, right?

**Jikumaru:**  
Ah, you noticed that. (Laughs) If you want an exhilarating jump on a wave, you need to be able to see the crest of the wave to gauge the timing of your jump. But with regular wave visuals, it's hard to tell where the crest of the wave is. That's why I asked for white foam, or whitecaps, to be added to the crests. I was like, "Hmm, I don't see any whitecaps on the waves...". Then the programmers would say, "How about now, Jikumaru-san?". And I'd be like, "I still can't see it! Just a little more!". We went back and forth like this for a while before the job was done. The programmers really worked hard. Thanks to that, I think jumping on waves has turned into a nice little gameplay element.

![Image 6: AtD18_Inserted_14.jpg](https://www.nintendo.com/eu/media/images/01_website_elements/other_elements/grey.gif)

### Was that also part of your commitment to user-friendliness?

**Jikumaru:**  
Yes. But while we continued to work on this, the designers started to request different ways to express water, not just from a gameplay perspective, but also in terms of the visual portrayal of beaches and shoals.

**Ishikawa:**  
I wanted to show the shoal floor through the crystal-clear water. At first, we were worried that we wouldn't be able to show the shoal floor because it was demanding on the processor. But our programmers made improvements here and there, and we were able to make it happen. Even with the familiar Koopa Troopa Beach course, we were able to create the visuals we wanted to show... Thank you for that, Sato-san.

**Sato:**  
Because we were so particular about this, the designers needed to toil away to make the shoal floor visible. (Laughs) But thanks to their efforts, it improved the quality of the graphics.

**Ishikawa:**  
You must’ve also worked hard to create the sound you hear when driving on water, right, Asahi-san?

**Asahi:**  
That’s right. Unlike driving on land, when driving on water, the vehicle bobs up and down along with the movement of the water. The sound is designed to correspond to the vehicle's movement and orientation. It was created with great attention paid to even the most delicate sounds, so please listen out for it when you're driving on water.

**[Continue to Chapter 4: A new generation of Mario Kart](https://www.nintendo.com/en-za/News/2025/May/Ask-the-Developer-Vol-18-Mario-Kart-World-Chapter-4-2832777.html "Ask the Developer Vol. 18, Mario Kart World – Chapter 4")**

Check out the rest of the interview
--------------------------------------

**  
Part 3: An interconnected world**
--------------------------------------

**You mentioned that the amount of content ended up increasing. You also drew a lot of concept art for this game.**

**Ishikawa:** The designers came up with various ideas, thinking that if the theme was a vast world, they could show things other than racing. There were sketches of characters, scenery, costumes that matched the various landscapes, characters eating... We had a vast, interconnected world in mind, so a good deal of the concept art depicted scenes of people’s lives there. We designed the costumes and vehicles as a set and created these poster-style designs.

![Image 1](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-18-mario-kart-world-part-1/Inserted/Inserted_10)

**Oh, even though it's** **_Mario Kart_****, there are some that show the characters eating food instead of driving a kart.**

**Yabuki:** The idea of showing characters eating a variety of foods came up early on in development.

**Jikumaru:** If you're traveling through a vast and diverse world, you can’t leave out the local food that's unique to each place. But actually, we did consider removing the food feature at one point. Incorporating it into the game means adding not only the food itself, but also the stores that sell it and the staff that work there, which would mean even more content.

**But you came back to this idea later?**

**Jikumaru:** Yes, while development was ongoing, about two years after the idea came up, I thought to myself, “You know what? I need food!” (Laughs) Unable to let it go, I asked the programmers to implement a hamburger model I'd created and make it so that the characters could eat it. It was well received within the team, and the designer started to churn out different kinds of food. Before we knew it, the number of variations had exploded.

**Ishikawa:** The designer in charge was really pumped up about creating them. We've incorporated lots of Mario-inspired twists and tidbits to create a wide variety of designs. I also had a lot of fun looking at those designs.

![Image 2](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-18-mario-kart-world-part-1/Inserted/Inserted_11)

**Sato**: Food is sold at “Yoshi's,” fictional drive-thru restaurants located all over the game's world. Yoshi and his friends make food inspired by each area.

**So, “Yoshi's” is a chain of drive-thrus that's expanded across the world.**

**Ishikawa**: Exactly. For example, a Yoshi's drive-thru located in a volcanic region would look like a volcano and sell piping-hot soup inspired by Bowser. (Laughs)

**Jikumaru**: As we were making these various concepts, Yabuki-san comes marching up to me and says, “When Mario eats something, he transforms.” He sounded pretty serious about it. (Laughs)

**Yabuki**: Originally, we were creating the various outfits separately from the foods. So, we wondered if we could combine those two elements.

**Oh, so the foods and outfits were unrelated at first?**

**Yabuki**: Yes, they were two completely separate elements. We discussed the idea of using coins to buy clothes from clothing stores, but that would have meant stopping at stores to shop, which would have disrupted the flow, given that this is a world where you can keep driving. That's when the idea of food came up. We thought, why don’t we have a drive-thru system where characters eat while driving, and eating makes them change outfits or transform into a different character? Though, it's utterly ridiculous. (Laughs)

**But in the world of Mario, it probably doesn't feel so strange.**

**Yabuki**: Then, the question came up: “Does Mario, in fact, eat mushrooms?” (Laughs)

**Jikumaru:** So in the midst of development, we went up to Tezuka-san (8) and asked him to confirm, “Is Mario actually eating those mushrooms?”

**(8)** _Takashi Tezuka. Executive Officer and Producer of the Planning & Development Division. Primarily involved in the development of 2D Mario games in the Super Mario Bros. series. Previously appeared in_ [_Ask the Developer Vol. 11, Super Mario Bros. Wonder._](https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-11-super-mario-bros-wonder-part-1/)

**Yabuki**: That's right. And Tezuka-san answers, “Yeah, he is.”

**Everyone**: (Laughs)

**Jikumaru**: Plus, the idea of eating food from a particular region and then changing into an outfit associated with that region fits the game perfectly. As you're racing, it's a real delight to see players changing one by one into the local outfit for that area.

**Yabuki**: Not all characters have outfits that change by eating food, but some have a variety that you can pick up while driving around and eating, so we hope this will be a good incentive for players to try out different characters.

**Now that you mention it, some of the new characters in this game seem like unlikely picks. I was surprised to see Cow as one of the playable characters.**

**Yabuki**: That's right. In previous games in the series, Cow was part of the scenery or an obstacle on one of the courses. But when we were working on an early version of a course in this game set on a ranch that players can drive through, this sketch came up. (Laughs)

![Image 3](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-18-mario-kart-world-part-1/Inserted/Inserted_12_updated)

**Oh, I thought Cow was just on the back of the truck, but she's actually driving it. (Laughs)**

**Ishikawa**: Each new _Mario Kart_ game features new characters to race with, but since we added so many to the previous game, we wondered where we could go from there. And then one of the designers came up with that silly sketch of Cow cruising along, and I thought to myself, “This is it!” (Laughs) So that's when we realized the course surroundings actually contained a lot of untapped resources.

![Image 4](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-18-mario-kart-world-part-1/Inserted/Inserted_13)

The character designer quickly put together a prototype of Cow that could race, and surprisingly it didn't feel out of place at all. So we thought maybe we could include other obstacle characters, and decided to add Cheep Cheep and Pokey as racers. As a result, the idea of taking obstacle characters, usually found in courses in past games, and having them participate in races made sense to me in terms of an interconnected world.

**Sato**: We called these types of characters “NPC drivers.” In other words, non-player character drivers.

**Yabuki**: So it was like, “They're NPCs, but they're playable? Which is it?” (Laughs) It's pretty funny to see a four-legged Cow holding onto motorcycle handlebars with her front hooves.

**Ishikawa**: But when she jumps, she strikes a proper quadrupedal pose. So I'm pretty sure Cow is still in touch with her animal nature. (Laughs)

**Jikumaru**: It was thanks to the introduction of various “NPC drivers” that the idea to have Kamek appear as an item was born. When Kamek casts a spell, the racers are transformed into playable NPCs, so one by one they might all turn into Cow mid-race. I think it turned out to be a unique item that has never been seen before. In fact, Cow is a character who's inspired a lot of different ideas, including obstacle characters like Camel and Giraffe.

**Ishikawa**: Cow is actually a pivotal character in the _Mario Kart_ series. (Laughs)

**Asahi**: On the other hand, when previously non-playable characters like Cow become playable, it means giving them new ways to express emotion, which must have been difficult for the voice lead. We were conscious of depicting the personalities and characteristics of “NPC drivers” in a way that doesn't look inferior to classic characters like Mario. The voice team members went through a lot of trial and error in the pursuit of the ideal sound. In addition to more characters, this game also has a wider selection of vehicles for characters to drive, so it was a huge task to create engine sounds that matched the characteristics, such as the appearance and structure, of each vehicle. We tried out a lot of different sounds in our search for something ideal—we even used croaking frogs and beating drums. (Laughs)

**Sato**: There are a lot of vehicles in this game, too. Since the game is about racing around the world, we've included not only race karts, but also everyday vehicles. It must have been tough for the designers, as they had to not only design the body of the vehicle, but also consider how the tires would transform when drifting and how the vehicle would move when jumping.

**I see. Because players are driving in a vast, interconnected world, you designed vehicles that can handle a variety of driving styles and circumstances.**

**Ishikawa**: That's right. For example, the Standard Kart has a higher ride height in this game, and suspension movement has been added so that when you drive it, the tires move in accordance with the unevenness of the surface and your actions.

Since players are driving in a vast world, we wanted them to enjoy racing not only on asphalt, like on a racetrack, but also on rough, off-road surfaces. This was made possible thanks to the programmers' careful attention to the vehicle movements. We also wanted it to be fun to choose a vehicle based on the world's different locations and situations, so we tried to make the lineup as varied and distinct as possible.

**In terms of the design, in the previous game,** **_Mario Kart 8 Deluxe_****, you drove underwater, but in this game, you can drive on water, right?**

![Image 5](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-18-mario-kart-world-part-1/Pop_Up/Popup_06)

**Sato**: Yes. Since you drive on water, we put a lot of effort into the wave graphics, too. Not just how they look—our up-and-coming programmers also implemented simulations, such as ripples spreading when something drops in the water, or waves appearing after a vehicle passes through. They made it possible to create waves on demand. This game has enemy characters that create waves when they attack, so we were able to incorporate players jumping on those waves into the gameplay.

**Jikumaru**: Racing on water is something this game has in common with the _Wave Race 64_™ (9) game.

**(9)** _Nintendo 64 software released in November 1996 in North America. Players race across the water on watercrafts at full throttle, competing for time and technique._

**Ishikawa**: That's right—when it came to the jumping action, Jikumaru-san, you were very particular about the whitecaps of the waves, right?

**Jikumaru**: Ah, you noticed that. (Laughs) If you want an exhilarating jump on a wave, you need to be able to see the crest of the wave to gauge the timing of your jump. But with regular wave visuals, it's hard to tell where the crest of the wave is. That's why I asked for white foam, or whitecaps, to be added to the crests. I was like, “Hmm, I don't see any whitecaps on the waves...” Then the programmers would say, “How about now, Jikumaru-san?” And I'd be like, “I still can't see it! Just a little more!” We went back and forth like this for a while before the job was done. The programmers really worked hard. Thanks to that, I think jumping on waves has turned into a nice little gameplay element.

![Image 6](https://assets.nintendo.com/image/upload/f_auto/q_auto/dpr_1.5/ncom/en_US/articles/2025/ask-the-developer-vol-18-mario-kart-world-part-1/Inserted/Inserted_14)

**Was that also part of your commitment to user-friendliness?**

**Jikumaru**: Yes. But while we continued to work on this, the designers started to request different ways to express water, not just from a gameplay perspective, but also in terms of the visual portrayal of beaches and shoals.

**Ishikawa**: I wanted to show the shoal floor through the crystal-clear water. At first, we were worried that we wouldn't be able to show the shoal floor because it was demanding on the processor. But our programmers made improvements here and there, and we were able to make it happen. Even with the familiar Koopa Troopa Beach course, we were able to create the visuals we wanted to show... Thank you for that, Sato-san.

**Sato**: Because we were so particular about this, the designers needed to toil away to make the shoal floor visible. (Laughs) But thanks to their efforts, it improved the quality of the graphics.

**Ishikawa**: You must’ve also worked hard to create the sound you hear when driving on water, right, Asahi-san?

**Asahi**: That’s right. Unlike driving on land, when driving on water, the vehicle bobs up and down along with the movement of the water. The sound is designed to correspond to the vehicle's movement and orientation. It was created with great attention paid to even the most delicate sounds, so please listen out for it when you're driving on water.

7.content:
And why the game's not called Mario Kart 9.
-------------------------------------------

Nintendo has discussed Mario Kart World's fan-favourite new character, Cow, and shown off the piece of concept art that secured her place in the game as a playable character.

Speaking as part of a fascinating [Ask the Developer](https://www.nintendo.com/us/whatsnew/ask-the-developer-vol-18-mario-kart-world-part-1/) interview, the [Mario Kart World](https://www.ign.com/games/mario-kart-world) development team revealed their "silly sketch" that convinced the game's development team to upgrade Cow from a background character to a fully-fledged part of the game's roster.

"In previous games in the series, Cow was part of the scenery or an obstacle on one of the courses," producer Kosuke Yabuki said. "But when we were working on an early version of a course in this game set on a ranch that players can drive through, this sketch came up."

The sketch, which shows a smiling Cow driving a truck and looking like she does not have a care in the world, was immediately seized upon as inspiration for Cow to become Mario Kart's next playable character — and led to other background NPCs becoming playable, too.

"Each new Mario Kart game features new characters to race with, but since we added so many to the previous game, we wondered where we could go from there," art director Masaaki Ishikawa continued.

"And then one of the designers came up with that silly sketch of Cow cruising along, and I thought to myself, 'This is it!' (Laughs) So that's when we realized the course surroundings actually contained a lot of untapped resources."

[![Image 1: Mario Kart World's Cow concept art.](blob:https://www.ign.com/b9a31d3949b1882a09ed2f8508d538f3)](https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2025/05/21/image-1747839986951.png)

Mario Kart World's Cow concept art. Image credit: Nintendo.

Cow's addition to the Mario Kart World roster was quickly followed by Cheep Cheep (the red fish Mario often has to dodge) and Pokey (the smiling, wiggling cactus character) also becoming playable.

"It was like, 'They're NPCs, but they're playable? Which is it?'" Yabuki continued. "It's pretty funny to see a four-legged Cow holding onto motorcycle handlebars with her front hooves."

"But when she jumps, she strikes a proper quadrupedal pose," Ishikawa added. "So I'm pretty sure Cow is still in touch with her animal nature. (Laughs)"

Elsewhere in the same interview, Yabuki confirmed that Nintendo had the name Mario Kart World in mind "from the early stages of development" when the game's open-world nature was already being worked on.

"If the idea had just been to add more courses, then I think we would've called it Mario Kart 9," Yabuki said. "But, that wasn't our approach this time. We wanted to take the series to the next level. So, we decided to drop the numbering this time and go with a completely new title."

### Mario Kart World Screenshots

Finally, the development team discussed Mario Kart World's addition of unlockable character costumes, found by snacking on food at Yoshi's drive-thru restaurants in different in-game regions.

Each region will unlock its own costumes, and offer its own food varieties. One example given is a Yoshi's drive-thru in a volcano region selling hot soup inspired by Bowser.

Originally, Nintendo says it hadn't linked its ideas for unlockable costumes and food together, with the former simply being planned to be purchasable from in-game shop locations. But stopping at these interrupted the game's open-world driving experience, developers said, and anyway — didn't Mario magically transform costumes already when he gobbled food up?

"The question came up: 'Does Mario, in fact, eat mushrooms?'," Yabuki laughed. The query prompted Mario Kart World's development team to hunt down Nintendo legend Takashi Tezuka, and get his verdict.

"Tezuka-san \[answered\], 'Yeah, he is'," Yabuki confirmed. And thus, Mario Kart World's costume-producing food was born.

Perhaps the biggest surprise to come out of the interview was the revelation that [Mario Kart World began development on Nintendo Switch, before performance concerns led to the game being delayed](https://www.ign.com/articles/mario-kart-world-began-development-on-switch-1-and-suffered-performance-struggles-until-switch-2-delay-offered-ray-of-hope) for launch on Switch 2 instead.

Mario Kart World, and Cow, will arrive on Switch 2 on the console's launch day — June 5, 2025.

8.content:
We're grilling Nintendo about this.
-----------------------------------

I feel like we've earned a reprieve today from the news chaos of tariffs and Nintendo Switch 2 pricing, so here's something fun (?) for your Friday: IGN played [Mario Kart World](https://www.ign.com/games/mario-kart-world) at a Nintendo event in New York this week, and confirmed that yes, the new Cow character can in fact eat burgers and steak (and many others things as well).

If you're wondering what on earth we could possibly be talking about, allow me to point you to the recent announcement of Mario Kart World, which included the introduction of the Moo Moo Meadows Cow as a playable racer. The Internet, of course, [is thrilled about this](https://www.ign.com/articles/you-can-play-as-the-moo-moo-meadows-cow-in-mario-kart-world-and-the-internet-is-thrilled), already coming up with dozens of memes and fanart of the adorable Cow that, until recently, was nothing more prominent than a fun background character in a single Mario Kart track.

However, as news of Cow spread throughout the land, fans began pointing out a potential, erm, problem, with another element of the Mario Kart World reveal. In the Nintendo Direct 2 trailer from Wednesday, Mario eats a burger. Burgers are (typically) made of beef. Would Cow, whose people are ostensibly a source of beef, consume beef herself? Fans really wanted to know.

Well at the Nintendo preview event, we found out. You see, the food items we saw in the trailer are obtainable in Mario Kart World at Yoshi's diner locations scattered across courses. They function like a drive-thru, allowing racers to drive up and grab a bag of take-out just like they would an item box. There are a lot of different food items that can be inside, including burgers, steak kebabs, pizza, and donuts.

And yes, Cow can eat them all.

> Yes, Cow CAN eat steak in Mario Kart World. [pic.twitter.com/qN5PZ9IIM4](https://t.co/qN5PZ9IIM4)
> 
> — IGN (@IGN) [April 4, 2025](https://twitter.com/IGN/status/1908259261769003473?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

During our session we also saw Cow eat a number of other items, including the burger. We're still a little hazy on what these items are actually doing for Cow — other racers change costumes when consuming them, but Cow doesn't seem to experience any effects. Could she be eating beef just because she enjoys it? Is there a secret power-up she gets from burger consumption that we just don't know about yet because Nintendo hasn't revealed it? Or perhaps are these veggie burgers and Beyond meat kebabs?

IGN reached out to Nintendo to try and clear all this up, but we haven't heard back yet. I'm sure it's because they're busy at their New York event, and not because this is an [unhinged question to ask](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o5RRyyHsjoU) their PR about. Yeah, that's probably it.

Anyway go check out our [preview of Mario Kart World](https://www.ign.com/articles/mario-kart-world-for-nintendo-switch-2-first-hands-on-preview), the [video version of which](https://www.ign.com/videos/mario-kart-world-for-nintendo-switch-2-first-hands-on-preview) features an appearance by our friend Cow.

_Rebekah Valentine is a senior reporter for IGN. You can find her posting on BlueSky @duckvalentine.bsky.social. Got a story tip? Send it to rvalentine@ign.com._
